title: Clinical Reasoning: Acute Abdominal Pain
prompt: A 30-year-old presents with acute abdominal pain that began this morning. Walk me through your structured approach — how you'd take the history, how the location and features shape your differential, the investigations you'd order, and your initial management.
blurb: A structured approach to acute abdominal pain — using location and features to build a differential, plus focused workup and safe management.

rubric.label: History & data gathering
rubric.description: Takes a systematic pain history (site, onset, character, radiation, timing, exacerbating/relieving, severity), associated GI/GU symptoms, gynecological and sexual history where relevant, and red-flag features; asks about medications, alcohol, and past surgery.

rubric.label: Differential diagnosis
rubric.description: Builds a differential organized by location/quadrant and by acuity, front-loading emergencies (ruptured ectopic, perforation, ischemic bowel, AAA, appendicitis with peritonism); always considers pregnancy in a person of childbearing potential.

rubric.label: Clinical reasoning
rubric.description: Uses history and exam (localization, peritonism, guarding, specific signs) to raise or lower diagnoses; explains discriminators; avoids anchoring; updates with new data.

rubric.label: Investigations
rubric.description: Orders a focused, justified workup — vitals, urinalysis, pregnancy test (mandatory when relevant), bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs, lipase/amylase, CRP, lactate, group & save), and targeted imaging (ultrasound vs CT) with rationale.

rubric.label: Initial management
rubric.description: ABC, IV access and fluids, analgesia and antiemetics, keep nil by mouth if surgical, sepsis screen and antibiotics when indicated; timely surgical/gynae referral; avoids masking or delaying a surgical abdomen.

rubric.label: Safety & prioritization
rubric.description: Screens for the unstable, peritonitic, or hemorrhaging patient early; mandatory pregnancy test; recognizes when this is a surgical emergency and escalates promptly.

rubric.label: Communication & structure
rubric.description: Presents reasoning in an organized, systematic way; thinks aloud; would communicate clearly and sensitively with the patient (including gynecological/sexual history).

reference.scenario: A 30-year-old with acute abdominal pain since this morning. The station tests a structured approach to the acute abdomen: a focused history, a differential organized by location and acuity that always includes pregnancy/ectopic in a person of childbearing potential, a justified workup, and safe initial management with appropriate escalation. The interviewer can add data (location, exam signs, a positive pregnancy test, unstable vitals) to test evolving reasoning. Content is generic and educational, not a real treatment protocol.
model_points: Starts by screening for the sick patient — ABC, vitals, signs of shock, peritonism — and treats those in parallel with assessment.
History: systematic pain characterization (SOCRATES); associated symptoms — nausea/vomiting, bowel habit change, blood in stool, dysuria/frequency, urinary or vaginal discharge; anorexia and fever.

Crucial context: last menstrual period and pregnancy possibility, sexual history, gynecological history; past abdominal surgery (adhesions), alcohol (pancreatitis), medications (NSAIDs, steroids), family history.

Uses location to structure the differential by quadrant: RUQ (biliary, hepatitis), epigastric (peptic ulcer/perforation, pancreatitis, MI), RLQ (appendicitis, ectopic, ovarian pathology, Crohn's), LLQ (diverticulitis, ectopic, ovarian), suprapubic (UTI, retention, PID), loin-to-groin (renal colic), diffuse/central (early appendicitis, obstruction, ischemia, gastroenteritis, DKA).

Front-loads life-threatening causes: ruptured ectopic pregnancy, perforated viscus with peritonitis, bowel ischemia/obstruction, ruptured/leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm, severe pancreatitis, and appendicitis progressing to perforation.
Mandatory pregnancy test in anyone of childbearing potential — an ectopic can present as undifferentiated abdominal pain and is immediately life-threatening.

Exam: localized tenderness, guarding, rebound/percussion tenderness (peritonism), specific signs (Murphy's, McBurney's, psoas), bowel sounds, hernial orifices, and a pelvic/gynecological assessment when indicated.

Investigations: vitals, urinalysis, urine/serum beta-hCG, FBC, U&E, LFTs, lipase/amylase, CRP, lactate, glucose, group & save; imaging targeted to suspicion — transvaginal/abdominal ultrasound (gynae, biliary, free fluid), CT abdomen/pelvis for many acute surgical presentations, erect CXR if perforation suspected.

Initial management: IV access and fluids, analgesia and antiemetics (analgesia does not obscure the surgical abdomen and should not be withheld), nil by mouth if a surgical cause is likely, sepsis screen and antibiotics when infection/perforation suspected, VTE assessment, and timely referral to surgery or gynecology.
Continual reassessment, clear escalation, and safety-netting; sensitive, private history-taking for sexual/gynecological questions.

probes.trigger: candidate omits a pregnancy test in a person of childbearing potential
probes.question: What single test would you not want to miss in a 30-year-old presenting like this, and why?

probes.trigger: candidate anchors on appendicitis without a broader differential
probes.question: What else could cause right lower quadrant pain here, and how would you tell them apart?

probes.trigger: candidate lists a differential without using pain location
probes.question: How does the location of the pain narrow your differential — walk me through it by quadrant.

probes.trigger: candidate proposes withholding analgesia to 'not mask' the exam
probes.question: Would you withhold pain relief while you assess? What does the evidence say about that?

probes.trigger: candidate gives a broad panel without justification
probes.question: Justify each investigation — what would a positive or negative result tell you?
The heart rate is 120, blood pressure 90/60, and the abdomen is rigid. What now?

red_flags: Failing to do (or mention) a pregnancy test in a person of childbearing potential.
Jumping to a single diagnosis (e.g., appendicitis) without a location-based differential.
Missing the immediately life-threatening causes (ruptured ectopic, perforation, ischemia, leaking AAA).
Not recognizing peritonism/instability as a surgical emergency needing escalation.
Withholding analgesia on the outdated belief it masks the surgical abdomen.
Ordering imaging or bloods with no rationale, or a scattershot panel without reasoning.
Insensitive or skipped sexual/gynecological history where it's clearly relevant.
follow_ups: The pregnancy test is positive and the patient is hypotensive with pelvic pain — what's your immediate concern and action?
How would your approach change if the pain were epigastric with a raised lipase?
What features would push you toward a CT versus an ultrasound first?
When would you involve the surgical team, and what would you hand over?
How would you sensitively take a sexual history from a patient who seems reluctant?
reference.exemplar_answer: I'd begin by screening for a sick patient — checking ABCs and vitals for shock and examining for peritonism — because an acute abdomen can be a surgical emergency, and I'd resuscitate in parallel with assessing. For the history I'd characterize the pain systematically with SOCRATES and ask about associated symptoms: vomiting, change in bowel habit, blood in stool, urinary symptoms, fever and anorexia. Critically, in a 30-year-old of childbearing potential I'd take a menstrual and sexual history and do a pregnancy test, because a ruptured ectopic can present as undifferentiated abdominal pain and is immediately life-threatening. I'd also ask about alcohol, NSAID use, and previous abdominal surgery. I use the location to structure my differential: right upper quadrant makes me think biliary; epigastric raises peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, even cardiac causes; right lower quadrant means appendicitis but also ectopic and ovarian pathology; left lower quadrant diverticulitis or gynae causes; loin-to-groin renal colic; and diffuse pain raises obstruction, ischemia or early appendicitis. Across all of these I keep the emergencies at the front — ruptured ectopic, perforation with peritonitis, bowel ischemia or obstruction, and a leaking aneurysm. On examination I'd localize the tenderness, check for guarding and rebound, look for specific signs like Murphy's or McBurney's, and do a pelvic assessment if indicated. Investigations: vitals, urinalysis, a beta-hCG, FBC, U&E, LFTs, lipase, CRP, lactate and a group & save, with targeted imaging — ultrasound for gynae or biliary questions, CT for many acute surgical presentations, and an erect chest film if I suspect perforation. Management runs alongside: IV access and fluids, analgesia and antiemetics — and I would give pain relief, since it doesn't mask a surgical abdomen — keeping the patient nil by mouth if surgery is likely, antibiotics if I suspect infection or perforation, and a timely referral to surgery or gynecology. I'd reassess continually and escalate early if the patient were unstable or peritonitic.

interviewer_notes: Mid-level clinical reasoning station. Watch for two non-negotiable safety behaviors: doing a pregnancy test in a person of childbearing potential, and recognizing peritonism/instability as a surgical emergency. Let the candidate build structure, then feed data — a positive pregnancy test with hypotension to test ectopic recognition, or epigastric pain with raised lipase to test flexibility. Reward a differential organized by location and by acuity, and reasoning that updates with new findings. Common weak points to probe: anchoring on appendicitis, omitting the pregnancy test, and the outdated instinct to withhold analgesia. This is a reasoning exercise, not a protocol recital; exact doses are not required, and the candidate should take sexual/gynae history sensitively.
